newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: India should change grain import policy - analyst.
newsitem.headline: India should change grain import policy - analyst.

text.p: India, faced with infrastructure bottlenecks, should export foodgrains from areas of supply surplus through the nearest ports and use the money earned to import at strategic locations to serve regions with chronic shortfalls, an analyst said on Thursday.

While continuing with the path of self-reliance, India should adopt this approach instead of transporting grains overland at high cost, T. Kundu, an official with the New Delhi-based Howe (India) Pvt Ltd, told a grains conference.
"The national planners, because of market-driven forces, are likely to have a closer look at this option and initiate development work in this direction," Kundu said.
India follows a policy of food management which stresses self-sufficiency and keeping foodgrains prices within the reach of the mass of the population.
Food and nutritional security has been largely interpreted to mean adequate availability of basic food products in the country as a whole.
India was a large wheat importer in the sixties and early seventies, but its output has since grown and the country exported wheat in 1996.
Exports were banned later last year after output fell and local prices soared. India has since imported wheat.
Kundu said the concept of food security needed to be broadened to include people's access to basic nutritional requirements, both physically and economically.

"The ongoing economic reform will accelerate the surfacing of the real cost of foodgrains at the destination. Sooner, the cost of indigenously produced grain at distant places may match or exceed that of imported grain"

India's state-run Food Corporation of India (FCI) buys about 99 percent of its wheat needs from five northern and central Indian states and roughly 90 percent of its rice from four northern states and one southern state.
FCI then transports most of the grains in bags by rail to remaining parts of the country for sale through the public rationing system.
But the movement of grain is often hampered by a lack of rail wagons availability, restricted storage space, and manual labour shortage at the source and destination.
India is a regular rice exporter but its wheat imports and exports have been sporadic.

Kundu said India should develop an overall national concept identifying the surplus and shortfall zones for different foodgrains, target countries for both export and import and integrate ports with rail and road networks.
Currently none of India's 11 major ports, barring the Jawaharlal Nehru Port near Bombay, is equipped with specialised mechanical grain handling facilities.
Kundu said the emerging model, envisaging large exports and imports, would require all-weather port facilities.
A government committee has identified five ports, two on the west coast and five on the east coast to concentrate on import and export of foodgrains in the next five years, he said.
